item.title: Teddi’s story: How a shared commitment to patient care keeps a senior dog moving.
item.dc:creator: Gray Media
item.description: Teddi, a senior dog rescued from the desert outside San Diego in 2012, has spent her life swimming in Mission Bay, paddleboarding off Oahu and hiking with her owners, Sarah and Jeff.
item.content:encoded:
Sponsored - The following content is created on behalf of Veterinary Emergency + Referral Center (VERC) and does not reflect the opinions of Gray Media or its editorial staff. To learn more about Veterinary Emergency + Referral Center (VERC), visit https://www.verchawaii.com.

Teddi, a senior dog rescued from the desert outside San Diego in 2012, has spent her life swimming in Mission Bay, paddleboarding off Oahu and hiking with her owners, Sarah and Jeff. So when Teddi’s legs began shaking and she started slowing down a few years ago, her care team at King Street Pet Hospital took notice.

As Teddi’s veterinarian, Dr. Audrey Bolaños had been monitoring her through regular wellness visits and monthly injections for arthritis. Over time, Dr. Bolaños noticed Teddi’s range of motion in her hips becoming more limited, sensitivity to touch and muscle wasting. These changes, combined with Teddi’s age and heart condition, suggested that medication alone wasn’t going to be enough.

“It’s about monitoring trends for patients and catching things early,” Dr. Bolaños says. “What may be small changes in [pet owners’] minds actually may be warning bells that we pick up on.”

Dr. Bolaños recommended physical rehabilitation at VERC (Veterinary Emergency + Referral Center of Hawaii).

“The referral process was very easy,” Sarah says. “They called me to schedule an appointment and were flexible.”

At VERC, Teddi first saw board-certified surgeon Dr. Chi-Ya Chen for a full exam and review of her medical history before starting a rehabilitation plan with technician Amy Honeychurch, CCRP, GDVA. The team explained the therapies available, asked about

Teddi’s symptoms and the family’s goals, and built a plan that included targeted exercises and acupuncture.

“We were surprised that there were so many options available,” Sarah says.

What sets Teddi’s care apart is how connected it has stayed. VERC shares Teddi’s progress with King Street through an online portal and email updates, giving Dr. Bolaños visibility into the exercises and goals guiding Teddi’s rehab.

“Communication with VERC is pretty easy,” Dr. Bolaños says. “I think goals are important, and communication helps achieve those goals.” Sarah agrees: “I love that they can share information. Both are very good with communication, and I feel like Teddi is in great hands.”

The results have been meaningful. Teddi’s legs have stopped shaking, she’s able to sit again, and she’s back to hiking Oahu’s shaded trails with her family.

“Seeing her get stronger was really rewarding,” Sarah says. “It motivated us to keep going.”

For Dr. Bolaños, Teddi’s progress is a reminder of what’s possible when a general practice and a referral hospital work as one team.

“Having access to VERC is a breath of fresh air,” she says. “It’s nice to be able to refer patients that need additional care I cannot provide, and owners are extremely thankful to find answers for their pets.”

item.title: Do you need to step back from caregiving? How to spot the signs
item.dc:creator: LeAnne Gendreau, Katherine Ambrose , Sondra 'Sam' Cradduck , Amy Amy Cameron O’Rourke, Rhea Rogers
item.description: We explore how to recognize when family caregiving demands have become too overwhelming and why stepping back can be the healthiest choice for everyone involved.
item.content:encoded:
(Aging Untold) — Caregiving is often called an act of love, but over time it can wear down your mind, your body and your relationships.

The Aging Untold experts explain the warning signs of caregiver burnout, why stepping back can actually be the safer choice and how to make the transition without falling into guilt.

“It’s OK if you’re even deliberating quitting”

Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, says the first step is giving yourself permission to admit you’re struggling.

“The first thing I would say is, it’s OK if you’re even deliberating quitting. And it’s very understandable,” O’Rourke said. “If you’re really, really tired, you’re not sleeping, everybody’s making you mad, and you’re getting burnt out — the first thing I would do is do whatever you need to do to get unburned out. Don’t make a decision in the middle of that stress.”

O’Rourke recommends caregivers step back, let someone else fill in and let their nervous system settle before making any long-term decision.

“Get your central nervous system kind of dialed back a bit, and then make the decision,” she said. “If you’re going to make the decision — I want to quit — then have a plan. What’s the transition plan? Is it a community? Is it a relative? Is it a paid caregiver, whatever it is.”

Expect “buyer’s remorse” after the decision

O’Rourke said caregivers who do step back should prepare for a wave of conflicting emotions afterward.

“Be fully prepared to what I call buyer’s remorse,” O’Rourke said. “You make the decision and then you regret it, and you’re back and forth. ‘I’m a bad daughter.’ ‘I couldn’t do it.’ So there’s some back-and-forth emotions. I’ve had clients do this and they end up quitting. And then I have others — they got the rest they needed, and then they went back and did it differently.”

Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, compared unmanaged caregiver stress to a fire waiting to happen.

“We often love to tell caregivers, don’t let yourself get burnout. But listen, guys — the match is lit, the kindling’s sitting there, and there’s literally gasoline on it,” Cradduck said. “And there’s not oftentimes water in the area to put the fire out. We fail to tell people how not to burn out.”

Respite care can offer a reset

Cradduck pointed to hospice respite care as one option for families whose loved one has reached that stage of care.

“If your loved one has reached the stage of hospice, hospice respite care is part of that program,” Cradduck said. “You can have your loved one, if they’re in the home, transported to a community for a week to 10 days. And they can do this every quarter. It can give you that reset and that break. And then you can go, ‘OK, I can do this a little longer.’ Or maybe you’re like, ‘You know what, I can’t.’”

O’Rourke added that respite care isn’t limited to hospice situations.

“If they’re not terminal, communities have respite care. Home health has respite care too,” O’Rourke said. “I love the idea of just saying, temporarily, I’m taking a leave of absence.”

Love doesn’t mean you have the ability to do the job

Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said one of the hardest parts of caregiving is separating love for a person from the physical and emotional capacity to care for them.

“Being a caregiver takes away from your identity over time,” Rogers said. “One of the hardships is understanding that love doesn’t mean ability. When you recognize that you’re at a crossroad, I think that’s really empowering, because if you continue to do what you know is not working out, you’re going to take it out on your body physically as well. And then the resentment comes in, and then that fight-or-flight — you’re stuck in this mode and you just can’t heal. It becomes detrimental to both parties.”

Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose shared what she has seen.

“I see people that say, ‘I loved my mom all the way to heaven. It was the greatest honor of my life,’” Ambrose said. “And then I see other people that say, ‘I can’t put my husband in a home. My children are ready to support me doing that, but I just can’t do it, and I don’t know what to do.’”

Ambrose noted that overwhelmed caregivers sometimes reach a point of hopelessness.

“Sometimes caregivers don’t outlive the person they’re caring for,” Ambrose said. “That’s sad when people are so overwhelmed that they may hope that they just pass away in their sleep, and that’s the way they see the burden being lifted.”

Caregiving doesn’t have to mean hands-on, 24/7 work

Ambrose said families should remind caregivers that stepping back from hands-on duties doesn’t mean stepping away from the relationship.

“Maybe mom needs even more than just, ‘Mom, we’re ready to support you when you’re ready,’” Ambrose said. “Maybe she needs to be rescued, because many caregivers do not outlive the spouse or the parent they’re caring for. But here’s the deal: Caregiving doesn’t have to be 24/7 hands-on. It can be advocacy and still being the spouse, still being the mom, still being the daughter.”

Ambrose described leverage as the key to sustainable caregiving.

“How can you use leverage? Leverage is three things: it’s systems, people and tools,” Ambrose said. “You may not know what those are, but you can reach out to people that work in home care, home health, the doctor’s office, the social worker at the hospital. Just keep asking questions, and you’ll find the resource to the resources. You’ll find your answers.”

Give yourself permission to get help

Cradduck said many caregivers stay in unsustainable situations because of a sense of duty tied to marriage vows or family roles.

“The problem that I see so frequently is the duty – It’s my duty. ‘Sickness and in health, better or worse — and this is the worst, and this is the sickness,’” Cradduck said. “I say you can still live those out as the spouse and not be the one that’s doing all the work. Try your darndest to find somebody that can help you out and give you that break. And then if that break’s what you need on a permanent level, go ahead and have somebody else step into the role. Give yourself permission. This is the hardest job you will ever do.”

Key takeaways

  • Love doesn’t automatically equal capacity. Being the closest emotionally or geographically doesn’t mean you’re the one who has to have the skills or ability to provide hands-on care.
  • Burnout harms both people — the caregiver and the person receiving care — through resentment, stress and physical health decline.
  • Stepping away may be the healthiest choice.
  • You can exit in planned stages — rest to clear your head, plan finances and arrange who will fill gaps in coverage.
  • Caregiving can mean advocacy, not just hands-on labor. Using “leverage” — systems, people and tools — can let you stay involved without doing everything yourself.

item.title: InvestigateTV+: A conservation success story
item.dc:creator: Michael Buckner
item.description: An American symbol once on the brink of extinction, the bald eagle is considered a conservation success story.
item.content:encoded:
(InvestigateTV) — An American symbol once on the brink of extinction, the bald eagle is considered a conservation success story. InvestigateTV+ explores its decades-long journey to recovery.

Then, we uncover the paper trail leading to a Russian citizen in Texas and why Medicare recipients should take a second look at their statements.

Plus, a father honors his son by teaching young drivers about the dangers on the road.

An American success story

A bald eagle sits atop a Louisiana cypress tree in Lake Palourde near Morgan City, a scene that would have been inconceivable a few short decades ago.

“We can see up to 60 eagles in a tour,” said Billy Gaston, who makes a living largely off providing eagle sightseeing tours in and near the lake.

The government removed the eagle from the Endangered Species List in 2007, widely regarded as one of conservation’s great success stories.

Read more

Investigation reveals Medicare billing scheme

A WSMV4 investigation has uncovered a Medicare fraud scheme that billed the federal program tens of thousands of dollars for medical supplies that Tennessee recipients never needed or received.

Our investigation found the billing is connected to a Russian citizen living in Texas, accused in a $3 billion Medicare fraud scheme.

Read more

item.title: This grocery store employee makes sure every customer finds what they’re looking for
item.dc:creator: Dale Ryman, InvestigateTV staff
item.description: For almost three decades, Greg Atchison has been a friendly face in the grocery business.
item.content:encoded:
WAUSAU, Wis. (InvestigateTV) - For almost three decades, Greg Atchison has been a friendly face in the grocery business.

“It’s greeting people. Meeting people, seeing people, it’s therapeutic,” Atchison said.

Atchison has worked 28 years in customer service. Twenty years at Festival Foods, formerly Trig’s, and eight at County Market. His approach extends beyond typical customer interactions.

Jake Sischo, store director at Festival Foods, said customers recognize Atchison immediately when they enter the store.

“It’s almost like ‘Cheers.’ Instead of yelling ‘Norm,’ they walk in and they’re like ‘Greg! How’s it going?’” Sischo said.

Dana Glaser, a Festival Foods customer, said Atchison consistently provides helpful service.

“He just always has a smile. If you can’t find what you need he’ll go in the back and get it for you and wrap it up,” Glaser said.

Atchison said his approach centers on genuine enthusiasm for the work.

“Come to work. You’re happy to be here. You’re happy to serve people. People see that. They pick up on it. It’s a 2-edge sword,” Atchison said.

His service earned him the company’s all-star boomerang award, which recognizes employees who encourage customer loyalty.

“It’s about bringing the guest back. Doing something that will make sure the guest comes back and enjoys shopping with us. That is what Greg does,” Sischo said.

Atchison was the second person in the store to receive the award and among the first 10 in the company, according to Sischo.

Customer Jerry Schroeder said Atchison consistently helps other shoppers.

“Always helping somebody. See. He’s down there helping somebody now,” Schroeder said.

Now in his early 70’s, his work schedule has been scaled back from full-time hours.

“Full-time retirement is full-time work to find yourself busy. To keep yourself busy. Especially when you don’t have hobbies,” Atchison said.

Customers continue to seek him out during his shifts.

“Because he’s always so cheerful. You’ve had a bad day, come in, and he’s happy. Smiling,” Schroeder said.

Sischo said the store will accommodate Atchison’s continued employment.

“We will take him for as long as he wants to be here,” Sischo said.

Atchison said he plans to continue working because of his passion for customer service.

“If you love what you do, it’s not work. And I love doing this. I really do,” Atchison said.

Festival Foods has a 10-tile policy requiring employees to greet customers within 10 tiles and offer assistance. Atchison extends that range, greeting customers from 20 or 30 tiles away.

media:content.media:description: For almost three decades, Greg Atchison has been a friendly face in the grocery business.

item.title: ‘Learn from Lutz’: Sharing his son’s traffic death to encourage safe-driving
item.dc:creator: Peter Zampa, InvestigateTV staff
item.description: Mike Lutzenkirchen created the Lutzie 43 Foundation after his son’s death in hopes of preventing fatal crashes caused by unsafe driving.
item.content:encoded:
GEORGIA (InvestigateTV) — Mike Lutzenkirchen is sharing his son’s story with teens and young adults in hopes of preventing fatal crashes caused by unsafe driving.

Lutzenkirchen’s son, Philip, died in a car accident in 2014. Philip, a former Auburn football player, had been drinking with friends before getting into a car. Investigators said the car was speeding and ran a stop sign, killing both Philip and the driver.

Both had blood alcohol levels above the legal limit.

“It’s just like that. There’s a crash last night. Your son is dead,” Mike Lutzenkirchen said, recalling a conversation with a coroner the day after Philip’s death.

“We went to a black hole for two weeks. We’re trying to figure out what do you do in life,” Lutzenkirchen said.

A new foundation

Lutzenkirchen created the Lutzie 43 Foundation after his son’s death. The foundation works with schools, government agencies and law enforcement to address the more than 42,000 annual traffic deaths in the United States.

The foundation holds summits, including one at Georgia Military College, where students take part in breakout sessions.

The foundation’s message asks drivers to take 43 seconds when they get in a car — a reference to Philip’s jersey number at Auburn — to make sure they have a clear head, clear hands, clear eyes, and to buckle their seat belt.

The summit also covers sharing the road with truckers and demonstrates how state transportation professionals and first responders work the scene of a crash.

School and law enforcement response

Georgia Military College Assistant Principal Jennifer Deason said students attending the summit are distracted by their phones and the freedom of driving, which leads them to ignore safety.

“Every student that attends here, I see them as my children. And so to know that they are in danger, if every time they get on the highway, whether or not they are distracted or not,” Deason said.

Capt. Maurice Raines, deputy director of the Georgia Governor’s Office of Highway Safety, said fatal crashes are 100% preventable.

“Hopefully by educating, the word will get out that we need to change our behavior. And if that doesn’t work, law enforcement will work to try to change that behavior,” Raines said.

Raines said more than 200 traffic deaths have occurred in Georgia so far this year.

Nationwide goal

Lutzenkirchen’s goal is a recognizable nationwide campaign sharing his son’s story.

“We’re trying to take the mistakes that Philip and his friend made that weekend and just make a difference. Live like Lutz, love like Lutz, and learn from Lutz,” Lutzenkirchen said.

The Lutzie 43 Foundation’s safe driving summit also demonstrates how state transportation professionals and first responders work a crash scene, allowing students to learn from multiple perspectives why driving is both dangerous and a privilege.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports seat belts can reduce the risk of death or injury by nearly half.

media:content.media:description: Father turns son’s traffic death into safe-driving mission

item.title: Ken Urker, Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s ex-fiancé, found dead on his birthday, reports say
item.dc:creator: Jack Meyer, Debra Worley
item.description: Ken Urker, ex-fiancé of Gypsy Rose Blanchard, was found dead in his Raceland, Louisiana, home on his 34th birthday, authorities and family confirm.
item.content:encoded:
RACELAND, La. (KPLC/Gray News) - Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s ex-fiancé Ken Urker was found dead in Louisiana, according to several reports.

He was 34.

A source close to the family confirmed his death to People. TMZ was first to report the news.

Urker’s brother Dylan found him unresponsive in his home on Thursday, which would have been his birthday, TMZ reported.

The Lafourche Parish Sheriff’s Office said officers were called to a home in Raceland around 6:15 p.m. and found Urker dead, according to People.

According to People, Urker’s sister went live on TikTok Thursday night, confirming his death. She said his last words to her were “I love you,” People reported.

Urker and Blanchard were engaged from October 2018 to August 2019 while she was still in prison for her role in killing her abusive mother.

The two later rekindled their romance in April 2024. The two welcomed a daughter, Aurora Raina Urker, that same December.

item.title: ‘He’s Not a Hero’: Sen. Fevella pushes state to challenge jury’s wrongful termination ruling
item.dc:creator: HNN Staff
item.description: At the State Capitol on Thursday, State Sen. Kurt Fevella strongly criticized the verdict and urged state attorneys to contest it.
item.content:encoded:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - An outspoken state lawmaker is urging the state to appeal a Honolulu jury’s verdict in favor of a former Hawaii Tourism Authority executive who sued for wrongful termination.

On Tuesday, a jury found Gov. Josh Green’s chief of staff, Brooke Wilson, liable for illegally firing Isaac Choy, the former HTA vice president of finance. Choy had filed a whistleblower lawsuit claiming he was terminated after raising concerns over the alleged misuse of agency resources.

Wilson and interim HTA Chair Caroline Anderson maintained Choy was fired for workplace violations, including making racist and sexist comments.

The jury awarded Choy $504,000 in total damages, including more than $454,000 in lost wages and $50,000 in punitive damages.

At the State Capitol on Thursday, State Sen. Kurt Fevella strongly criticized the verdict and urged state attorneys to contest it.

“You guys got to understand, this means a lot to me. Growing up in Hawaii, Hawaiian communities, Hawaiian families were discriminated against for decades upon decades,” he said. “I’m asking the State of Hawaii to challenge and appeal this discrimination and womanizer for what he is. He’s not a hero. He’s a zero.”

Fevella argued that if anyone else, including himself, used any kind of racial or sexist comments, they would face immediate fallout.

“If it was you, me saying those kinds of things, if I had used any racial slurs or discriminated against women in this square building, you guys would’ve asked for my resignation, you’d have this building impeach me and get rid of me,” he said.

The jury awarded Isaac Choy, a former legislator and HTA executive, $504,000 in damages, including more than $454,000 in lost wages and $50,000 in punitive damages.

The state Department of the Attorney General previously defended Wilson and the HTA, noting that officials disagree with the jury’s decision and are reviewing legal options, including an appeal.

item.title: First Alert Forecast: Flash Flood Warning for northern half of Kauai
item.dc:creator: Dan Cooke
item.description: At 8pm, Tropical Storm Nolo was 455 miles WNW of Lihue with winds of 65 mph. It was moving WNW at 6 mph. Nolo is forecast to regain hurricane strength over the weekend, but will be far enough away that its influence on our weather will finally end.
item.content:encoded:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - At 10:50 p.m., the National Weather Service issued a Flash Flood Warning for the northern half of Kauai until 1:45 a.m. Friday.

Doppler radar and automated rain gauges indicated heavy rain falling over the northern half of Kauai. Rain was falling at a rate of 1 to 2 inches per hour. Flash flooding is ongoing or expected to begin shortly.

A Flood Advisory remains for the rest of Kauai until 1 a.m. Friday.

A Flood Advisory means minor flooding is ongoing or expected to begin shortly. Rain was falling at a rate of 1 to 1.5 inches per hour over the southern half of the island. You are encouraged to stay away from streams, drainage ditches and low-lying areas prone to flooding.

At 8 p.m., Tropical Storm Nolo was 455 miles WNW of Lihue with winds of 65 mph. It was moving WNW at 6 mph. Nolo is forecast to regain hurricane strength over the weekend, but will be far enough away that its influence on our weather will finally end.

Friday will be a transition day, with winds moving from ESE to ENE. That slight change will make a lot of difference as the ENE trade winds will usher in a much more stable atmosphere, drier conditions, sunnier skies, with just a few passing showers... mainly windward and mauka, nighttime and mornings.

Weekend weather should be very nice. We will enter a period of wetter trades on Monday that will last through the week and perhaps into next weekend.

item.title: Court tosses manslaughter sentence after AI video of road-rage victim used in court
item.dc:creator: Mitchell Koch
item.description: The sentencing judge noted “obvious forgiveness” expressed in Pelkey’s AI statement before handing down the punishment.
item.content:encoded:
CHANDLER, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) — A convict will have to be resentenced after the Arizona Court of Appeals vacated his sentence because an AI video of the victim affected the judge’s decision.

Gabriel Horcasitas was sentenced to 10 1/2 years in prison last year for the road-rage killing of Christopher Pelkey in November 2021.

The victim’s family created an AI video of Pelkey using a previously recorded video, a picture and a script written by his sister. That video was played during the sentencing.

The sentencing judge noted “obvious forgiveness” expressed in Pelkey’s AI statement before handing down the punishment to Horcasitas.

During the sentencing, the judge said he “loved” the video and that Pelkey was able “to speak from his heart” as the family envisioned.

In its decision announced Wednesday, the state Court of Appeals said the sentencing judge was prejudiced by the AI video, which made his decision fundamentally unfair.

The Court of Appeals said Horcasitas’ manslaughter conviction is upheld, but the 10 1/2-year sentence is vacated and he will be resentenced.

media:content.media:description: Gabriel Horcasitas (left) will be resentenced in the November 2021 shooting death of Christopher Pelkey after the court of appeals found issue with an AI video of Pelkey played in court.

item.title: State reaches settlement with Monsanto over PCB contamination
item.dc:creator: Ben Gutierrez
item.description: The state had sued Monsanto and two of its affiliates over contamination caused by the synthetic chemical compounds.
item.content:encoded:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - The state Attorney General has announced a settlement with Monsanto Company and two of its affiliates over contamination caused by PCBs in Hawaii waterways and natural resources.

PCBs, or polychlorinated biphenyls, are man-made organic chemicals that were used in a wide variety of products until they were banned in 1979 following mounting evidence that they were toxic to human health and the environment.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency says PCBs were once in everything from electrical equipment and motors and sealants and paper products, and could still be in old oil-based paints and plastics.

“PCBs, they’re very persistent, they don’t break down in the environment,” said Wayne Tanaka, chapter director of the Sierra Club Hawaii.

“They are very, very toxic. They are associated with cancers, tumors, developmental issues with children who are exposed through their mothers,” he added.

Monsanto was the sole manufacturer of PCBs in the U.S. from the 1930s until 1977, when it voluntarily ceased production.

The ag giant has now agreed to pay the state $10 million, and potentially up to $35 million more, depending on the outcome of other PCB-related legal actions.

State Rep. Amy Perruso is vice chair of the House Committee on Energy and Environmental Protection. She praised the attorney general for securing the settlement, but was not satisfied with the amount.

“This settlement, I would say, is minimal, considering the extent of the damage and the length of the time period in which we experienced that damage,” said Perruso.

In a statement, Monsanto said, “During the time of manufacture, Monsanto conducted hundreds of studies on PCB safety, provided appropriate warnings to its sophisticated industrial customers based on state-of-the science at the time and cooperated with the U.S. government’s 1972 interdepartmental study.”

The company also said, “Additionally, data reported to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency about PCB impairments of waterways show that PCBs in the environment are generally declining 45 years after production ceased.”

The settlement doesn’t contain any admission of liability or wrongdoing by Monsanto.

“If corporations were actually treated as persons, this person would be in jail,” said Perruso.

“For me as a father of a young child, I worry, right?,” said Tanaka. “What am I exposing her at the beach? Can I take her fishing? Can we eat the fish that I used to enjoy, knowing now that these chemicals could be persistent in the environment?”

The settlement said the funds will be used for restitution and remediation for alleged harms due to PCB contamination, but a spokesperson for the attorney general said there are no specific projects or programs yet.

media:content.media:description: The saga began in September 2020 when the Burlington School District found PCB contamination in the nearly 1,000-student high school, ultimately deciding to permanently shutter and then demolish the campus and sending kids to a converted former Macy’s department store downtown in the meantime.

item.title: Shopper describes chaotic scene after truck plows through Hilo Longs Drugs
item.dc:creator: HNN Staff
item.description: Video from the scene showed the pickup truck completely inside the store, dislodging merchandise aisles as glass and debris scattered across the floor.
item.content:encoded:
HILO (HawaiiNewsNow) - Shoppers at a Longs Drugs on Hawaii Island had a scary moment when a truck came crashing through the storefront Thursday afternoon.

Rebecca Dudoit was shopping inside the store on Puainako Street at around 4 p.m. when she heard the impact.

Video from the scene showed the pickup truck completely inside the store, dislodging merchandise aisles as glass and debris scattered across the floor.

Dudoit said two people were on the ground, a cashier appeared in pain, and a man was pinned between a register and the car.

“It’s really scary, especially when I still have the scene in my eyes about the guy underneath the truck with it. All I could see was legs and slippers. I still see that in my mind,” she said.

Dudoit said store management evacuated customers until first responders arrived.

Hawaii News Now has reached out to county officials and the Longs Drugs store and is awaiting a response.

media:content.media:description: Video from the scene showed the pickup truck completely inside the store, dislodging merchandise aisles as glass and debris scattered across the floor.

item.title: New Biosecurity Academy aims to boost inspector ranks
item.dc:creator: HNN Staff
item.description: The state is launching a new Biosecurity Academy with Leeward CC to train up to 20 inspectors to protect Hawaii from invasive pests and diseases.
item.content:encoded:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - The state said it’s looking for new biosecurity inspectors to help in the never-ending fight against invasive species across Hawaii.

The Hawaii Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity (DAB) announced Thursday it is partnering with Leeward Community College’s (Leeward CC) Office of Workforce Development to accept the first students into the Biosecurity Academy.

Up to 20 recruits will be selected for the five-month program that starts in November.

Sharon Hurd, DAB chair, said the new academy will provide a flexible path for graduates looking for a position as a biosecurity inspector.

“This innovative program will allow the Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity to address the needs of the community by bringing in more inspectors to check cargo at airports and harbors and provide fast response to any pressing needs on the invasive species front across the state,” Hurd said.

The department said graduates will eventually work for DAB’s Plant Quarantine Branch (PQB). The branch was established in 1888 under King David Kalakaua to prevent pests from damaging island-grown coffee. PQB currently screens incoming passengers and cargo at airports and harbors for pests and microorganisms in fruits, vegetables and seafood headed to stores and restaurants.

State Sen. Donovan Dela Cruz called the Biosecurity Academy a great example of workforce development in action.

“By creating a direct pathway into meaningful careers, this program helps prepare the next generation of biosecurity professionals right here at home, while strengthening Hawaii’s ability to protect our agriculture and natural resources, bolster our biosecurity infrastructure and diversify our economy,” Dela Cruz said.

Applications open Saturday, Oct. 3, and those interested can sign up online once recruitment officially opens at 12:01 a.m.

Officials said applicants must have a four-year college degree. The Leeward CC Biosecurity Academy will provide training for the incoming state inspectors.

“Partnering with the Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity allows us to leverage our expertise in workforce development to build a highly trained pipeline of biosecurity inspectors,” said Carlos Penaloza, chancellor of Leeward CC and interim chancellor of the University of Hawaii at West Oahu. “This academy isn’t just about filling critical job vacancies; it’s about providing meaningful career pathways for our local talent while actively safeguarding our agriculture, natural resources and local economy for generations to come.”

media:content.media:description: The Hawaii Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity is looking to train new inspectors to help stop invasive species from entering the islands.

item.title: Mother charged with capital murder in deaths of 2 sons
item.dc:creator: Joe Villasana
item.description: Jail records show Colleen Lemmon is charged with two counts of capital murder.
item.content:encoded:
WAXAHACHIE, Texas (KWTX/Gray News) — A Texas mother is facing two counts of capital murder after authorities said she shot and killed her sons Thursday morning.

Forty-two-year-old Colleen Nichole Lemmon of Waxahachie was booked into the Wayne McCollum Detention Center following treatment at a local hospital for non-life-threatening injuries.

Deputies respond to 911 call

Ellis County Sheriff’s Office deputies responded around 4:13 a.m. Thursday to a 911 call reporting an unknown emergency at a home in the 900 block of Big Sky Drive in Waxahachie.

Deputies entered the home and discovered two male victims suffering from gunshot wounds.

One victim, identified by authorities as 21-year-old Christopher Scott Pitre of Waxahachie, was pronounced dead at the scene.

The second victim, a 15-year-old boy, was rushed to a local hospital in critical condition, where he later died from his injuries. The sheriff’s office said the teenager’s identity is being withheld.

Investigation and statement

Detectives developed probable cause through corroborating evidence recovered during the investigation that Lemmon was responsible for shooting both of her sons, the sheriff’s office said.

The victims’ father has been notified of both deaths.

“My deepest sympathies go out to the victims’ father, family members, and loved ones involved in this tragic incident,” Ellis County Sheriff Brad Norman said in a statement. “They will remain in our prayers during this difficult time.”

Jail records show Lemmon is charged with two counts of capital murder. Her bond is pending arraignment.

item.title: Poipu resort recovery: Major resort, vacation rentals face extensive damage from Hurricane Lowell
item.dc:creator: Mahealani Richardson
item.description: Nearly a month after Hurricane Lowell pounded Kauaʻi’s south shore, popular resort beaches normally packed with sunbathers remain desolate as recovery efforts get underway.
item.content:encoded:
POʻIPŪ, Kauaʻi (HawaiiNewsNow) - Nearly a month after Hurricane Lowell pounded Kauaʻi’s south shore, popular resort beaches normally packed with sunbathers remain desolate as recovery efforts get underway.

At the Sheraton Kauaʻi Resort in Poʻipū, the landscape has been completely altered. An empty swimming pool sits filled with ocean sand, surrounded by heavy machinery, orange construction fencing, and stacked banquet chairs.

Dramatic footage captured during the storm by a visiting CBS News crew showed powerful waves invading the property. Storm surge rushed into the resort, flooding the fitness center, interior courtyard, and lobby areas.

“We are inside the lobby of a hotel right now and we just had a huge wave wash ashore,” CBS correspondent Carter Evans reported as seawater swept into the building.

Extensive damage across South Kauaʻi properties

Local residents and business operators are grappling with the scale of destruction left in Lowell’s wake.

“It is kind of shocking. I’m used to it being very pristine,” said Shari Olson, who manages vacation and long-term rental properties on the island. “It’s encouraging to see that there are a lot of hands that are trying to put the island back together, especially the harder-hit areas like the south shore.”

Olson expressed concern regarding the island’s recovery.

“My heart hurts a little bit,” Olson said. “Not because it’s my industry. It’s because my heart is here with Kauaʻi.”

Just adjacent to the Sheraton, a row of oceanfront vacation rentals suffered catastrophic impacts. Inside one battered unit, floodwaters pushed kitchen fixtures entirely across the room, leaving living spaces packed with sand, mud, and splintered furniture.

“I can’t imagine if I was the owner of this property. It’s pretty overwhelming,” Olson said. “It’s going to take a lot of time and a lot of money to restore the property.”

The Kiahuna Plantation management reported damage to 17 units, including 10 oceanfront condos. Officials there aim to reopen non-oceanfront backside bungalows by Oct. 1.

The Sheraton Kauaʻi Resort’s booking portal currently shows no reservations available until early December.

Mixed reactions from island residents

While the drop in tourism strains local businesses, some residents note an unexpected sense of quiet across the south shore.

“To be honest, this is the second best thing that happened since COVID,” said Joshua Smazik of ʻŌmaʻo. “It got everybody away and the island time to breathe.”

media:content.media:description: Crews use heavy equipment to cleanup sand from the Sheraton Kauai Resort in Poipu.

item.title: Inside Jade Food: The family crafting Hawaii’s favorite crack seed for over 60 years
item.dc:creator: Jolanie Martinez
item.description: Inside the production facility, Jade Food President Deanne Ho oversees every step of the meticulous, labor-intensive preparation.
item.content:encoded:
WAIPAHU (HawaiiNewsNow) - Tucked inside an industrial warehouse along Koaki Street in Waipahu, the rhythmic sound of agitating water and soaking seed carries on a local tradition that has spanned more than six decades.

For Hawaii residents, crack seed is a nostalgic staple of island life. At Jade Food, preserving that heritage is a daily, hands-on family effort that began more than 60 years ago.

Good Old Manual Labor

Inside the production facility, Jade Food President Deanne Ho oversees every step of the meticulous, labor-intensive preparation.

“We are back to good old manual labor,” Ho explained. “We’re just over here agitating just so we can get the salt out from the seed. And then after we do this, we let it sit, and then we’re going to change the water. Depending on how the seed is, you might have to change it twice, but at least once more.”

Jade Food carries more than 50 varieties of treats, ranging from traditional rock salt and dry lemon peel to li hing mango and pickled mango—the latter requiring two to three weeks of marinating before it is ready for packaging.

For Ho, quality control is both personal and essential.

“I grew up eating crack seed,” Ho said. “I eat it every day. I try all the batches. It’s my job.”

A Pivot from Pizza to Seed

The company’s beginnings trace back to 1961, when Ho’s father, Hollis Ho, set out to launch a business. He originally considered selling pizza, but found consumers unready for the concept at the time.

“He tried to sell pizza, but he was a little bit too early on the wave because people were like, ‘Why would we pay for bread and tomato sauce and cheese?’” said Taelyn Tyau, treasurer at Jade Food and Hollis’ granddaughter. “So, then he eventually landed on crack seed because, you know, he wanted something that like no one else was doing.”

Remarkably, Hollis did not personally eat crackseed. To build his catalog, he traveled to Taiwan alongside a family aunt to sample recipes from local factories. He eventually brought experienced cooks over to teach him the craft.

Over time, Jade Food refined the original formulas to cater directly to local palates.

“We’ve adapted the seed to a more local taste,” Deanne Ho said. “Before, it had a more oriental, I would want to say, Chinese medicine taste. And we’ve made it a more mellow seed, more adaptable to Hawaiians, and it’s been like that for decades.”

As for the company moniker? While family lore often links it to the aunt who helped scout recipes in Asia, Hollis maintained a different inspiration.

“The person that he took to the Orient, her name was Jade, but my dad swears up and down that’s not where the name for Jade Food came from,” Deanne laughed. “He said he wanted a Chinese name and something that was precious, so he settled on the name Jade Food.”

Preserving a Vanishing Craft

Learning the trade meant working through every facet of the enterprise, from managing payroll and books to operating forklifts, driving delivery routes, and ultimately learning seed-making.

Today, Ho worries about the future of the craft as master makers age across the globe.

“The batches vary from batch to batch, so you constantly need to try the product,” Ho said. “It’s a really older generation thing. All the people who are making seed in the Orient are older. So, I encourage you guys to eat the seed and get the taste now, because who knows—in 20, 30 years, not that many people will be making it and it’ll be a really hard product to get.”

Now, a third generation is stepping up to carry the torch. Tyau works alongside her mother, motivated by the deep-seated nostalgia the brand evokes in customers across the islands.

“What keeps all of us going is our customers and our community,” Tyau said. “When people come up to us, and they’re like, ‘I grew up on Jade, and I love your stuff, reminds me of my childhood’—that’s really what keeps us going.”

item.title: Hundreds take to Honolulu streets for 32nd annual Men’s March Against Violence
item.dc:creator: HNN Staff
item.description: Hundreds marched through downtown Honolulu on Thursday for the 32nd annual Men’s March Against Violence, calling on men to help end domestic abuse.
item.content:encoded:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - Hundreds walked through downtown Honolulu Thursday morning for the 32nd annual Men’s March Against Violence.

Coinciding with Domestic Violence Awareness Month, survivors, advocates, community organizations, schools, and elected leaders walked in support of those impacted by domestic violence.

The march began at Iolani Palace for a remembrance, then traveled down King Street to Bishop Street, down Beretania Street, past the State Capitol and arrived back at the palace for a rally.

Kerrie Urosevich, CEO of the Domestic Violence Action Center, called on all men to help hold others accountable.

“When you hear something that isn’t right, whether it’s among your friends, your co-workers, in your community, speak up, hold each other accountable so men play a really critical role, and I also want to say I know many men and boys are victims of violence, so it’s ending violence for everybody,” she said.

If you or someone you know needs help, call the Domestic Violence Action Center’s helpline at 808-531-3771.

Click here for more resources from the DVAC. Donations can also be made to help support the nonprofit’s efforts.

item.title: ‘Ignored red flags’: Attorney for Moanalua HS victim says school, DOE failed to protect student athletes
item.dc:creator: Lynn Kawano
item.description: Attorneys say five more potential victims have come forward against ex-Moanalua wrestling coach Sean Sakaida as a family prepares to sue the state DOE.
item.content:encoded:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - Federal prosecutors said five more potential victims have come forward in recent days against Moanalua High School’s former girls wrestling coach, Sean Sakaida. That’s according to Sean Fitzsimmons, one of the attorneys representing the first girl to report alleged criminal activity by the 44-year-old.

Her family is now preparing civil action against the school and the Hawaii Department of Education.

“It’s clear that there’s more people out there. And we encourage people to contact the FBI and report any allegations,” Fitzsimmons said.

Attorneys cite ignored warning signs

Fitzsimmons said the school and the Department of Education ignored red flags.

That includes a 2012 investigation into Sakaida for reported inappropriate conduct at Roosevelt High School. Sakaida publicly denied wrongdoing at the time, and Moanalua hired him the following year.

“In our view, the decision to give Sakaida access to students after the Roosevelt allegations reflects a deeply troubling set of institutional priorities. It shows that Moanalua cared more about the success of its athletic program than the safety of its own students,” Fitzsimmons said.

Sakaida was arrested last week and is charged with possession of child pornography. He is being held at the Federal Detention Center without bail.

Second coach cited in prior hiring

Fitzsimmons also pointed to Moanalua’s hiring of Dwayne Yuen as an assistant boys basketball coach in 2011, despite prior restraining orders which are public record and misconduct allegations against Yuen at Punahou School.

Both were coaching at Moanalua in 2013.

Yuen is serving 33 years in federal prison for child exploitation. He pleaded guilty in December 2024 to committing crimes against three minor victims, including sex trafficking, coercing and enticing a minor to engage in sexual activity, and producing, receiving, and possessing child pornography.

“It’s unfathomable for me for a school to hire two coaches at the same time who had these allegations,” Fitzsimmons said.

No timeline was provided for the civil lawsuit. Fitzsimmons said they are waiting to see if more charges are filed because of the additional victims who came forward.

The Hawaii Department of Education said they do not comment on pending or active litigation but did say background checks are done that includes a fingerprint-based state and FBI criminal history record check. Arrests, criminal charges, court case numbers and final case dispositions are part of that check, “which the Department reviews to determine an individual’s suitability to work in close proximity to children,” a spokesperson said.

Sakaida’s preliminary hearing is set for Oct. 13.

item.title: ‘Disgusting’: Cleanup crew describes sights, smells inside damaged Happy Days
item.dc:creator: Aalii Dukelow
item.description: The crew tasked with cleaning the damaged Happy Days restaurant in Kaimuki gave a firsthand account of their efforts to remove rotting food trapped inside.
item.content:encoded:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - The crew tasked with cleaning the damaged Happy Days restaurant in Kaimuki gave a firsthand account of their efforts to remove rotting food trapped inside the establishment, weeks after its roof collapsed in August.

“Oh, it smells, it smells pretty bad,” said Aaron Ward, manager of 24 Hour Flood Pros, the company contracted to clean the eatery.

Many passersby agreed the smell coming from the property is pungent.

“(The smell) sours your stomach a little bit, it smells like rotting fish or rotting food, like a garbage dump,” said area resident Donald Bell.

A 24 Hour Flood Pros crew was dumping the rotting food on Thursday, while covered head to toe in protective yellow suits and donning respirators.

“There’s a lot of sludge that leaked out of the food, from the decaying food, and there’s oil and there’s just a lot of disgusting things that we deal with,” Ward added.

Besides dealing with the decaying dim sum and putrid meat since they began cleanup Tuesday, workers said the festering food has not attracted too many live animals.

“I think they (Happy Days) kept everything sealed off pretty well, so we’re not dealing with any of that, it’s more just the food waste,” Ward said.

While handling the food waste, 24 Hour Flood Pros did not let its workers remain in the building, covered in workwear, for more than 30 minutes.

“I guess this is what we do every day, we’ll have jobs like this,” Ward added.

Restaurant regulars, such as area resident Annie Lockwood, are happy the group is getting the job done as they wait for the day the business could reopen.

“I live just on Wilhelmina, and this was a great place that my family and I liked to come for celebrations. I had one of my birthdays there growing up, so it’s really sad to see what happened,” Lockwood said.

It is unclear if or when Happy Days will resume operations, as the property owner has not decided whether to repair or demolish the building.

Cleanup is expected to continue through Friday.

item.title: Firefighters contain fire at ABC Junkyard in Waiawa after explosions reported, advisory lifted
item.dc:creator: Ben Gutierrez, HNN Staff
item.description: Firefighters reported a large pile of miscellaneous recyclable material was burning.
item.content:encoded:
WAIAWA (HawaiiNewsNow) - Honolulu firefighters have contained a fire that broke out in Waiawa Wednesday afternoon at ABC Towing & Parts (ABC Junkyard), an auto salvage yard with a history of code violations and prior fires.

According to the Honolulu Fire Department, firefighters responded shortly before 3 p.m. to the property along the 800 block of Lehua Avenue.

Nearby residents reported hearing explosions coming from the facility as crews arrived on scene.

“There was a lot of explosions, big ones, you know,” said Andre Perez. “I can imagine acetylene tanks, something like that. Big, loud explosions.”

“There was probably at least eight, and then I left, I wasn’t going to stick around,” said Corrie Young. “I was scared, yeah. Really big explosions.”

Firefighters reported a large pile of miscellaneous recyclable material was burning. Wind from the south sent columns of thick black smoke over the H-1 Freeway and into Pearl City.

“Most of that trash looks synthetic. So this fire — the smoke was probably really toxic and it’s something that we’ve been expressing concern about for a long time, for over a year,” said Perez.

HFD said a total of 11 fire companies, including crews from Honolulu and federal fire agencies, responded to the fire.

“We’re lucky that it happened on rainy day,” said Camille Kalama, another neighboring resident. “Hopefully that helped dampen the fire. But this shouldn’t be happening in a neighborhood with residents all around us.”

The fire was contained just before 5 p.m. Crews will continue to perform overhaul tactics to search for hidden fires to prevent rekindling.

No injuries have been reported.

Smoke advisory

The Hawaii Department of Health has lifted a smoke advisory that went into effect Wednesday for parts of Pearl City due to the fire at ABC Towing.

DOH environmental health staff monitored conditions at ABC Towing & Parts and surrounding areas throughout Wednesday afternoon and evening, as well as this morning. According to officials, air monitoring indicates that air quality is at safe levels.

While the fire has been contained, it is not fully extinguished.

DOH advises residents to remain vigilant and continue to monitor conditions around the property.

If smoke is observed, residents should take precautions to limit exposure, including staying indoors, closing windows and doors — and setting air conditioning systems to recirculate. Individuals with respiratory or heart conditions, as well as children and older adults, should take extra precautions.

Anyone experiencing symptoms such as headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion, shortness of breath or chest pain should seek medical attention as appropriate.

DOH will continue to be on-site at ABC Towing today to monitor fire response, air quality conditions and conditions at Waiawa Stream.

DOH will provide additional information if conditions change.

Community response

Neighbors were concerned that the dump is still operating, since they mentioned there was a cease-and-desist order.

“It’s permitted to be a junkyard for cars, automotive junkyard. But it’s been turned into a landfill where they’re receiving truckloads of roll-off dumpsters every day with mixed trash, construction trash,” said Perez.

“We’re getting bombarded by the smoke, by dust on a daily basis, by the noise, and just by the threat of having this illegal landfill right next door,” said Kalama.

The junkyard owner has said that he is still allowed to operate while he appeals the orders.
